A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same time-horizon study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original AI-agent evaluations, human baselines, failure analyses, and internal pull-request and filename-perturbation experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains those original empirical studies and adds results for newer models and an inference-cost analysis.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains human-time difficulty ratings, task-specific success thresholds, diversity weighting, logistic horizon estimation, and regression against release dates. The revised IRT explanation does not change this method or the documented agent scaffolds.

E1.justification: Both versions use HCAST, RE-Bench, SWAA, SWE-bench Verified, internal pull-request tasks, and the modified local-document-search scenario. New model evaluations do not introduce additional tasks or domains.

E2.justification: v3 adds o3 and o4-mini to the evaluated model comparisons, including Figures 3–4 and Table 7. The six-model SWE-bench Verified comparison and three-model internal pull-request comparison retain their comparator sets.

E3.justification: Appendix H.3 adds evaluation of weighted success against allowed cost per run, including human reference curves. This extends v1's comparison of successful-run costs with human salaries. Primary scoring and baselining procedures remain unchanged; increased token budgets or reruns are not established.

E4.justification: v3 adds an inference-cost sensitivity check showing that most models with cost data plateau below their maximum allocation (Figure 18). Existing messiness, failure, filename-randomization, and methodological robustness analyses are retained, with some updated model results.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports p = 0.006 for o3 lying above the long-term trend. Approximately eight runs per agent-task pair and 10,000 hierarchical bootstrap samples remain the stated practices; no increase in repeated runs is documented.

E6.justification: v3 adds o3's approximately 110-minute horizon, o4-mini results, per-suite success scores in Table 7, and cost-response curves. The 50% horizon doubling estimate changes from 212 days (95% CI 171–249) to 207 days (166–240), and the 80% estimate changes from 213 to 204 days. These refits use an expanded model set; Table 7 reports no SWAA scores for o3 or o4-mini.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix C.4 corrects the mathematical explanation of the 50% horizon: h_agent = t_task yields success probability σ(0) = 0.5, replacing v1 Appendix B.4's inconsistent condition α = β_iη. The IRT mapping is rewritten coherently, while the proposed regression remains unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract updates the current-frontier claim from Claude 3.7 Sonnet at around 50 minutes to o3 at around 110 minutes, and the conclusion revises forecast dates. The proposed metric, approximately seven-month doubling claim, and conditional projection of month-long software-task automation remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive discussion of the method's advantages and tradeoffs relative to IRT, including foregoing task-level Fisher-information measures. It also discusses information loss from multistage estimation and possible end-to-end alternatives. Most human-context and external-validity limitations are retained through relocation.

D1.justification: v1 provides public reproduction code/data, task, scaffold, and transcript links. v3 removes these and instead promises partial supplementary code/data and additional figure code on reviewer request; task access becomes request-based. Conversely, Appendix C.3.2 newly discloses CPU and H100 compute totals. These are substantial changes to reproducibility information, without establishing changes in actual compute settings.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to StableToolBench, the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard, MLE-bench, DSBench, SWE-Lancer, and metabench. It expands the comparison with IRT, while retaining the central positioning of human-time horizons as an interpretable measure across capability levels.

P1.justification: The main narrative is extensively condensed and reorganized. Detailed related work, methods, qualitative analyses, external-validity studies, and discussion move into expanded appendices, with substantial rewriting of their main-text summaries. The title also adds 'Software'.

P2.justification: v3 merges v1 Figures 3 and 4 into a two-panel Figure 3, compresses and rearranges the logistic-fit panels, redraws trend graphics, and relocates many displays. It adds the per-suite results table and inference-cost figure, while removing the baseline-time-source table as a separate display.

improvement.justification: The corrected mathematical explanation, added budget-sensitivity check, and newer-model evidence improve aspects of the paper. However, reproduction access instructions become substantially more restrictive, and v3 introduces conflicting forecast endpoints: mid-2031 in the introduction versus mid-2030 in the conclusion. These material benefits and drawbacks leave the overall quality direction uncertain.
